steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a journal version of our paper on SOFT, a softmax-free linear-complexity Transformer for vision. Explain the quadratic-complexity bottleneck of self-attention in ViTs, why existing linear-attention approximations fall short, what SOFT does, our contributions, and how this version extends the earlier conference paper.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recently the big step change that Transformers brought in natural language processing (NLP) seems to have come to vision as well. Convolution neural networks (CNNs) have more inductive bias in their architecture design, and pure Vision Transformer (ViT) and its variants, which have less, have been shown to outperform CNNs on various vision tasks. But any Transformer based model has a bottleneck, which is its quadratic complexity in both computation and memory usage. This comes from the self-attention mechanism itself. Given a sequence of tokens as input (e.g., words or image patches), the self-attention module learns the feature representations iteratively by relating each token to all the other tokens. This gives a quadratic complexity O(n^{2}) with the token sequence length n in both computation (time) and memory (space), because an n\times n sized attention matrix has to be computed and saved during inference. The problem is especially bad in vision, because a 2D image after tokenization produces a much longer sequence than in NLP, even at a moderate spatial resolution. So this quadratic complexity stops a ViT model from modeling images at high spatial resolutions, and these are often crucial for visual recognition tasks.

The natural solution is to reduce the complexity of the self-attention computation by approximation. There have been a number of attempts at this in NLP. For example, one method takes a naive approach and shortens the length of Key and Value with learnable projections. This kind of coarse approximation will inevitably cause performance degradation. On the other hand, two other methods both use the kernel mechanism to approximate softmax normalization and so linearize the computation in self-attention. Another one uses a hashing strategy instead to selectively compute the most similar pairs. Recently, a further method uses Nyström matrix decomposition to reconstruct the full attention matrix, with polynomial iteration to approximate the pseudo-inverse of the landmark matrix. However, softmax normalization is just duplicated across the matrix decomposition process, which is not theoretically sound. We found empirically that none of these methods work well when applied to vision (see Sec. 4.1).

- SOFT
  - limitation is softmax self-attention; first softmax-free Transformer
  - softmax on top of scaled dot-product in all existing Transformers (cite); hinders linearization
  - SOFT: linear complexity O(n) in space and time; Gaussian kernel similarity, no softmax
  - low-rank matrix decomposition; Newton-Raphson for Moore-Penrose inverse
- Contributions
  - (I) softmax-free Transformer, linear space/time; (II) decomposition with theoretical guarantee
  - (III) backbone family with SOFT; longer token sequences (Figure 1b); beats CNNs and ViT variants on ImageNet (cite), accuracy/complexity (Figure 1a)
- Extensions over conference version (NeurIPS 2021 spotlight, cite)
  - (i) iterative inverse in forward only, gradient once in backward
  - (ii) spectral norm analysis; (iii) second-order spectral norm growth, fails in dense vision
  - (iv) normalized softmax-free self-attention; (v) ImageNet (cite), COCO (cite), ADE20K (cite)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recently the big step change that Transformers brought in natural language processing (NLP) seems to have come to vision as well. Convolution neural networks (CNNs) have more inductive bias in their architecture design, and pure Vision Transformer (ViT) and its variants, which have less, have been shown to outperform CNNs on various vision tasks. But any Transformer based model has a bottleneck, which is its quadratic complexity in both computation and memory usage. This comes from the self-attention mechanism itself. Given a sequence of tokens as input (e.g., words or image patches), the self-attention module learns the feature representations iteratively by relating each token to all the other tokens. This gives a quadratic complexity O(n^{2}) with the token sequence length n in both computation (time) and memory (space), because an n\times n sized attention matrix has to be computed and saved during inference. The problem is especially bad in vision, because a 2D image after tokenization produces a much longer sequence than in NLP, even at a moderate spatial resolution. So this quadratic complexity stops a ViT model from modeling images at high spatial resolutions, and these are often crucial for visual recognition tasks.

The natural solution is to reduce the complexity of the self-attention computation by approximation. There have been a number of attempts at this in NLP. For example, one method takes a naive approach and shortens the length of Key and Value with learnable projections. This kind of coarse approximation will inevitably cause performance degradation. On the other hand, two other methods both use the kernel mechanism to approximate softmax normalization and so linearize the computation in self-attention. Another one uses a hashing strategy instead to selectively compute the most similar pairs. Recently, a further method uses Nyström matrix decomposition to reconstruct the full attention matrix, with polynomial iteration to approximate the pseudo-inverse of the landmark matrix. However, softmax normalization is just duplicated across the matrix decomposition process, which is not theoretically sound. We found empirically that none of these methods work well when applied to vision (see Sec. 4.1).

In this work we identify that the limitations of the existing efficient Transformers come from using softmax self-attention, and we propose a softmax-free Transformer for the first time. More specifically, all existing Transformers (with or without linearization) need a softmax normalization on top of the scaled dot-product between token feature vectors. Keeping this softmax operation makes any later linearization efforts difficult. To get past this obstacle we introduce a new softmax-free self-attention mechanism called SOFT, which has linear complexity O(n) in both space and time. Specifically, SOFT uses a Gaussian kernel to define the similarity (self-attention) function, so there is no need for a softmax normalization afterwards. With this softmax-free attention matrix we also introduce a new low-rank matrix decomposition algorithm for the approximation. The robustness of the approximation is theoretically guaranteed by using a Newton-Raphson method to reliably compute the Moore-Penrose inverse of the matrix.

Our contributions are the following. (I) We introduce a new softmax-free Transformer that has linear space and time complexity. (II) We approximate the attention matrix with a new matrix decomposition algorithm that has a theoretical guarantee. (III) To evaluate the method on visual recognition tasks, we design a family of generic backbone architectures of different capacities that use SOFT as the core self-attention component. Extensive experiments show that because of the linear complexity (Figure 1b), our SOFT models can take much longer image token sequences as input. As a result, with the same model size, SOFT outperforms the state-of-the-art CNNs and ViT variants on ImageNet classification in the accuracy/complexity trade-off (Figure 1a).

A preliminary version of this work was presented as a NeurIPS 2021 spotlight. In this paper we extend the conference version further in the following ways: (i) We make computing the Moore-Penrose inverse more efficient and robust by using an iterative method only in the forward process and calculating its theoretical gradient only once in backward propagation. (ii) We analyze the limitations of the preliminary SOFT from the perspective of the matrix spectral norm, which shows that normalization is important for improving the model's task generalizability. (iii) We prove that in the preliminary SOFT the matrix spectral norm increases to second order relative to the matrix size, which makes it fail in dense vision problems. (iv) To address these limitations we propose a normalized softmax-free self-attention, which keeps linear complexity and improves performance, and this is supported by both theoretical proof and extensive experiments. (v) The improved SOFT outperforms the state-of-the-art CNNs and ViTs for classification on ImageNet, object detection on COCO and semantic segmentation on ADE20K.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recently the step change brought by Transformers [11] in natural language processing (NLP) [15,16] seems to have arrived in vision [7,8,17,18]. Indeed, with less inductive bias in its architecture design than Convolution neural networks (CNNs), pure Vision Transformer (ViT) [7] and its variants have been shown to outperform CNNs on various vision tasks [19,20]. However, every Transformer based model has a bottleneck, namely its quadratic complexity in both computation and memory usage. This is intrinsic to the self-attention mechanism: given a sequence of tokens (e.g., words or image patches) as input, the self-attention module iteratively learns the feature representations by relating one token to all other tokens. This results in a quadratic complexity O(n^{2}) with the token sequence length n in both computation (time) and memory (space), since an n\times n sized attention matrix needs to be computed and saved during inference. The problem is particularly acute in vision: a 2D image after tokenization produces a far longer sequence than those in NLP, even at a moderate spatial resolution. This quadratic complexity therefore prevents a ViT model from modeling images at high spatial resolutions, which are often crucial for visual recognition tasks.

A natural solution is to reduce the complexity of the self-attention computation via approximation. Indeed, there have been a number of attempts in NLP [12,14,21,13]. For example, [12] takes a naive approach of shortening the length of Key and Value via learnable projections. Such a coarse approximation inevitably causes performance degradation. In contrast, [14,22] both leverage the kernel mechanism to approximate softmax normalization in order to linearize the computation in self-attention. [21] instead adopts a hashing strategy to selectively compute the most similar pairs. Recently, [13] uses Nyström matrix decomposition to reconstruct the full attention matrix, with polynomial iteration for approximating the pseudo-inverse of the landmark matrix. Nonetheless, softmax normalization is simply duplicated across the matrix decomposition process, which is theoretically unsound. We found empirically that none of these methods is effective when applied to vision (see Sec. 4.1).

In this work, we identify that the limitations of existing efficient Transformers are caused by the use of softmax self-attention, and for the first time we propose a softmax-free Transformer. More specifically, in all existing Transformers (with or without linearization), a softmax normalization is needed on top of the scaled dot-product between token feature vectors [11]. Keeping this softmax operation challenges any subsequent linearization effort. To overcome this obstacle, we introduce a novel softmax-free self-attention mechanism, named SOFT, with linear complexity O(n) in both space and time. Specifically, SOFT uses a Gaussian kernel to define the similarity (self-attention) function without the need for a subsequent softmax normalization. With this softmax-free attention matrix, we further introduce a novel low-rank matrix decomposition algorithm for approximation. The robustness of the approximation is theoretically guaranteed by employing a Newton-Raphson method to reliably compute the Moore-Penrose inverse of the matrix.

We make the following contributions. (I) We introduce a novel softmax-free Transformer with linear space and time complexity. (II) Our attention matrix approximation is achieved through a novel matrix decomposition algorithm with a theoretical guarantee. (III) To evaluate our method on visual recognition tasks, we design a family of generic backbone architectures with varying capacities that use SOFT as the core self-attention component. Extensive experiments show that, with linear complexity (Figure 1b), our SOFT models can take much longer image token sequences as input. As a result, with the same model size, SOFT outperforms the state-of-the-art CNNs and ViT variants on ImageNet [1] classification in the accuracy/complexity trade-off (Figure 1a).

A preliminary version of this work was presented as a NeurIPS 2021 spotlight [23]. In this paper, we further extend the conference version as follows: (i) We improve the efficiency and robustness of computing the Moore-Penrose inverse by using an iterative method in the forward process only, while calculating its theoretical gradient only once in backward propagation. (ii) We analyze the limitations of the preliminary SOFT from a matrix spectral norm perspective, revealing the importance of normalization for enhancing the model's task generalizability. (iii) We prove that the preliminary SOFT experiences a second-order increase in matrix spectral norm relative to the matrix size, which makes it fail in dense vision problems. (iv) To address these limitations, we propose a normalized softmax-free self-attention that keeps linear complexity while enhancing performance, supported by both theoretical proof and extensive experiments. (v) The improved SOFT outperforms the state-of-the-art CNNs and ViTs for classification on ImageNet [1], object detection on COCO [24] and semantic segmentation on ADE20K [25].
